newsitem.title: GERMANY: Opel denies reports of job cuts, lower profits.
newsitem.headline: Opel denies reports of job cuts, lower profits.

text.p: Car-maker Adam Opel AG, the German unit of U.S. carmaker General Motors, on Wednesday denied a magazine report that it planned to cut nearly 7,000 jobs in Germany up to the year 2000.
A report in the latest edition of Capital magazine said that Opel was expecting net profits to fall in 1997 to 120 million marks from 315 million the previous year.

Opel said in a statement that the figures released in the report were theoretical planning figures, which could be affected by the performance of the economy in the meantime and could easily be subject to change.

The carmaker went on to say that speculation of a fall in earnings was "totally premature, given that auditors are still examining profit figures and balance sheets for 1996, which Opel will report on June 19."
Opel said in February that there would be increased pressure on sales, production and earnings in 1997.
Capital magazine said jobs at the group's factories in Ruesselheim, Bochum and Kaiserslautern could as a result be affected. The group currently employs around 45,000 people in Germany.
According to the magazine article, Opel revised its sales outlook for 1997 to 30 billion marks, down from 31.2 billion, on 1.48 million cars sold instead of 1.61 million cars.
In 1996 Opel reported turnover of 28.3 billion marks, up 9.3 percent on the previous year.
The report said that Opel planned a further rise in net profits to 350 million marks, while sales will remain at current levels of 30.4 billion marks.
